title: Learn REST API design basics
why: APIs are the contract between the UI, other ERP modules and your service.
steps: Watch the REST video, then the API best practices video.
Read the Stripe idempotency article. It explains how to stop double processing.
Look up pagination and error format only when you need them.

resources.note: Video, about 6 min. Resources, verbs, status codes.

resources.label: ByteByteGo: API design best practices

resources.label: Stripe: Designing robust APIs with idempotency
resources.note: Read all of it (8 min). Same idea protects your statement upload.

resources.label: Google AIP-158: Pagination
resources.note: Skim. Why cursor (page token) beats offset for large lists.

resources.label: Stripe API: Errors

resources.label: Microsoft REST API Guidelines
resources.note: Reference only. Look things up, do not read it all.

title: Write the endpoints for bank reconciliation
why: Apply what you learned to your real feature while it is fresh.
steps: In Doc 1 §5, list 5–6 endpoints, for example:
POST /bank-statements (upload, with Idempotency-Key)
GET /bank-statements/{id} (processing status)
GET /bank-statements/{id}/lines?status=unmatched&cursor=…
POST /statement-lines/{id}/match and DELETE /statement-lines/{id}/match
POST /bank-statements/{id}/finalize
For each: request body, response, and 2 error codes.
Answer: what happens if the same file is uploaded twice?

title: Recall: the 9 thinking questions
why: Spaced recall, day 1. Writing from memory is what makes it stick.
steps: Without looking, write the 9 questions to ask about any feature.
Then check them against the chat plan and fix what you missed.

title: Learn data modelling and SQL vs NoSQL
why: The data model is the part of a design that is hardest to change later.
steps: Watch the SQL vs NoSQL video.
Read Accounting for Developers Part I. It is the double-entry ledger your Books module is built on.
Skim normalization: 1NF, 2NF, 3NF, and when to denormalize.

resources.label: ByteByteGo: SQL vs NoSQL
resources.note: Video. When to choose each one.

resources.label: Modern Treasury: Accounting for Developers, Part I
resources.note: Read. Accounts, debits, credits, double-entry. Directly relevant to Books.

resources.label: Hussein Nasser: database normalization
resources.note: Video. Pick one under 20 min.

resources.label: System Design Primer: RDBMS section
resources.note: Skim: replication, federation, denormalization.

title: Draw the tables for bank reconciliation
steps: Tables to design: bank_accounts, bank_statements, statement_lines, reconciliation_matches.
Link matches to your existing invoices, bills or journal entries.
Every table gets org_id. Money as integer minor units (paise) plus currency.
Statuses: statement (uploaded, parsing, ready, finalized); line (unmatched, suggested, matched).
Think: one bank line can pay many invoices. That is why the matches table exists (N:M).

title: Recall: API design
steps: From memory: 5 status codes and when to use them.
Explain idempotency keys in 2 lines.
Cursor vs offset pagination: one line each.

title: Learn how database indexes work
why: A missing index is the most common reason an ERP page gets slow.
steps: Read chapter 1 of Use The Index, Luke. It is short and has diagrams.
Read the concatenated keys page: column order in a composite index matters.
Watch the index video if reading feels heavy.

resources.label: Use The Index, Luke: Anatomy of an index
resources.note: Read chapter 1 only. B-trees and leaf nodes.

resources.label: Use The Index, Luke: Concatenated keys
resources.note: Read. Why (org_id, date) is different from (date, org_id).

resources.label: ByteByteGo: database indexing
resources.note: Video alternative if you are tired.

resources.label: PostgreSQL: Using EXPLAIN
resources.note: Skim the first examples. Seq Scan vs Index Scan.

title: Pick an index for each reconciliation query
steps: List the 3 main queries in Doc 1. For each, write the index that serves it.
Example: unmatched lines of a statement → (org_id, statement_id, status).
Example: candidate invoices to match → (org_id, amount_minor, due_date).
Run EXPLAIN on one real query in your Books database. Screenshot it as proof.

title: Catch up, then a 10-minute recall
why: Buffer day. Carried-over tasks come first. If there are none, just do this recall and rest.
steps: Finish any carried-over tasks above this one.
From memory, write 3 bullets each on: API design, data modelling, indexing.

title: Learn caching strategies
why: Caching makes reads fast, but stale data in finance is dangerous. Learn both sides.
steps: Watch both ByteByteGo caching videos.
Read the AWS caching best practices page.
If Books uses Spring, skim the Spring caching guide to see @Cacheable.

resources.label: ByteByteGo: Cache systems every developer should know
resources.note: Video. Where caches sit: browser, CDN, app, database.

resources.label: ByteByteGo: Top caching strategies
resources.note: Video. Cache-aside, write-through, write-back.

resources.label: AWS: Caching best practices
resources.note: Read. TTLs, invalidation, thundering herd.

resources.label: Spring guide: Caching data
resources.note: Optional. How to add a cache in Spring Boot.

title: Decide: does reconciliation need a cache?
steps: Write "Cache: yes or no, and why" in Doc 1 §7. "No, because…" is a strong answer.
Note 2 lines for Doc 2: reports are read-heavy, so where would a cache help, and when must it be cleared?

title: Recall: indexing and data modelling
steps: Explain a composite index and why column order matters.
Name the 4 reconciliation tables and how they connect.

why: An ugly full draft beats a perfect half draft.
steps: Problem, goals and non-goals (e.g. non-goal: live bank feeds).
Requirements with numbers: e.g. 10k lines per statement, matched within 2 minutes.
Architecture diagram in Excalidraw: UI → API → database, plus workers.
Paste in your API and data model work from Days 2–4.

title: Draft Doc 1: sections 7–12
steps: Trade-off ideas: parse in the request vs in a background job; exact rules vs fuzzy matching.
Alternatives: manual-only matching; using a third-party reconciliation tool.
Failure modes: corrupt file, duplicate upload, worker crash halfway.

resources.label: System Design Primer
resources.note: Use the index to look up anything you get stuck on.

title: Learn message queues, Kafka and the outbox pattern
why: Parsing 10k bank lines is too slow for one request. Queues let it run in the background safely.
steps: Watch the queue video and the Kafka video.
Read the transactional outbox page. It is the same idea as in the payment design.
Read what a dead-letter queue is.

resources.label: ByteByteGo: Message queues explained
resources.note: Video. Producers, consumers, why go async.

resources.label: ByteByteGo: Why is Kafka fast / Kafka explained
resources.note: Video. Topics, partitions, consumer groups.

resources.label: microservices.io: Transactional outbox
resources.note: Read. Save to the database and publish an event without losing either.

resources.label: Apache Kafka: Introduction
resources.note: Skim "Main concepts and terminology".

resources.label: AWS SQS: Dead-letter queues
resources.note: Read the first section. The idea applies to Kafka too.

title: Add the async flow to Doc 1
steps: Flow: upload → store file → outbox event "statement.uploaded" → Kafka → parser worker → save lines → matcher worker → notify user.
Consumers must be idempotent: the same event twice must not create duplicate lines.
Bad file → retries, then dead-letter queue, then status "failed" shown to the user.
Update the diagram.

title: Send Doc 1 to your senior for review
why: Review can take 2–4 days. Sending today keeps you on schedule.
steps: Share the doc and ask: "Could you review this design doc by early next week? I would value feedback on the trade-offs."
Proof: a screenshot or link of the message.

title: Learn how systems scale
why: Reports read millions of ledger rows. You need to know what breaks first and how to fix it.
steps: Watch the scaling video.
Learn the latency numbers and how to do a rough estimate.
Skim Postgres partitioning and materialized views. Both matter for reports.

resources.label: ByteByteGo: Scale from zero to millions of users

resources.note: Read "Powers of two" and "Latency numbers".

resources.label: PostgreSQL: Table partitioning

resources.label: PostgreSQL: Materialized views
resources.note: Skim. Precomputed results, a form of summary table.

title: Estimate scale for the reports engine
steps: Estimate: number of orgs, ledger rows per org per year, report requests per day, peak time (month-end).
Decide: compute reports from raw entries, or keep monthly balance snapshots? Write the trade-off.

title: Learn multi-tenancy models

steps: Skim the AWS whitepaper diagrams: silo, pool, bridge.
Read the Postgres row-level security page intro.
Watch a short multi-tenancy video.

resources.note: Skim the silo, pool and bridge model sections and their diagrams.

resources.note: Read the intro and first example. The database enforces org_id for you.

title: Write the tenancy section for Doc 2
steps: Find out how your ERP isolates tenants today (check the code or ask a teammate).
org_id leads every index on report tables. Write why.
Noisy neighbour: a big org exporting 5 years of data must not slow others. Answer: queued exports with a per-org limit.

title: Recall: scalability
steps: Vertical vs horizontal scaling: one line each.
What does a read replica help with, and what is its catch?

title: Learn API security basics
why: Financial data needs strong access control and an audit trail.
steps: Read the OWASP API Top 10 headlines. Read item 1 (BOLA) fully.
Read the JWT introduction.

resources.note: Read the list. Read API1 (Broken Object Level Authorization) fully.

resources.note: Read. What is inside a token and what is not secret.

resources.label: OWASP: Authorization cheat sheet
resources.note: Skim. Deny by default, check on every request.

title: Add security to both docs
steps: Roles: who can upload, reconcile, finalize, view reports, export.
Every query filters by org_id from the token, never from the request body.
Audit log for match, unmatch and finalize.
Encrypt uploaded statements; exports use expiring download links.

API: GET /reports/trial-balance?from&to, POST /reports/exports, GET /reports/exports/{id}.
Data model: ledger_entries plus account_period_balances (monthly snapshot).
